extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices that lead journals and publishers to investigate and retract published papers (e.g., evidence of fabrication, lack of ethical approval, publisher response and transparency). Useful for people assessing retraction causes and publisher behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overwhelming evidence of fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction at the request of the Editors-in-Chief “as a result of overwhelming evidence of fabrication, related to the fact that the distributions of many variables reported ... could not have occurred by chance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When statistical or other analyses show that reported data distributions are essentially impossible by chance, journals may treat that as overwhelming evidence of fabrication and retract affected articles. The retraction statement should explain the finding and the basis for action. Example from Clinical Therapeutics: the journal explicitly cited impossibility of reported distributions as the reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability of institutions to attest to study/data integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction justification included “the inability of Dr Fujii’s institutions to attest to the integrity of the study and/or its data conducted under their auspices.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the author’s institutions cannot verify or attest to the integrity of the research or underlying data, that lack of institutional confirmation can support a retraction. Journals often attempt independent and collaborative requests for verification; failure to obtain required information may lead to retraction of remaining manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to obtain proper ethical approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Some articles were retracted “at the request of the author,” for failing to obtain proper ethical approval before conducting the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research conducted without necessary ethics/IRB approvals is grounds for retraction. Such retractions can be initiated by authors or journals and should be clearly noted in the retraction notice (e.g., retracted due to lack of ethical approval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of retracted studies rendering a review/article scientifically unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: A review was retracted because it cited 14 of the author’s own studies which have all since been retracted; “This has rendered the content of the review scientifically unreliable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a review or secondary article relies on multiple studies that are later retracted and those retractions affect the review’s conclusions, the review itself may be considered scientifically unreliable and subject to retraction after investigation. Whistleblower reports can trigger such investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical analysis to detect improbable/fabricated results
rubrics_metrics.description: An anesthesiologist used statistical tools to determine the odds the results were likely to have come from actual experiments; the answer was described as ‘infinitesimally small.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical forensics (e.g., analyses of reported distributions, p-value patterns, improbability of dataset features) are a recognized method for detecting potential fabrication. Robust statistical evidence of impossibility can prompt editorial investigations and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/editorial responsibility and timeliness (avoidance of administrative oversight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elsevier attributed delays in implementing retractions to “human(s) error,” changes in the Journal Manager and editorial board, and called it an administrative oversight; other journals blamed editorial oversight for delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and editorial offices are expected to process retraction decisions in a timely manner; staff turnovers and procedural lapses that delay corrections are treated as administrative/editorial failures. Notices may include apologies and explanations, but journals bear responsibility to follow through once issues are identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of whistleblowers/third-party notifications in prompting investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: A whistleblower notified the Editor-in-Chief that a review included references to retracted articles, leading to a detailed investigation and eventual retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External reports from whistleblowers, readers, or other researchers commonly initiate or accelerate investigations into suspected problems. Journals should have procedures to assess such reports and undertake detailed investigations when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notices should state reasons and process
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction texts in these cases explicitly state causes (fabrication, inability to verify data, lack of ethical approval) and note whether retraction was at editors’ or author’s request; one notice also apologised for delay due to administrative oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent retraction notices that clearly state the reasons for retraction, who requested it, and any relevant procedural context (e.g., investigations, institutional responses, delays) are a best practice. Clarity helps readers understand the scope and cause of the correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated editorial actions (joint determinations) can lead to multiple retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to a ‘Joint Editors-in-Chief Request for Determination Regarding Papers Published by Dr. Yoshitaka Fujii’ initiated in 2012, which led to recommendations for many retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When concerns affect multiple articles across a field or author, coordinated actions by editors (joint determinations, cross-journal reviews) can be used to evaluate and implement retractions systematically. Such coordinated efforts may exclude certain article types (e.g., some review articles) and should be documented.
